title: Cold rebuild: base62 codes
summary: Rebuild the shortener's base62 encoder and decoder from memory, no hints.

steps.title: Cold rebuild
body: Time to prove a piece stuck. You wrote **base62 codes** in *Design a URL shortener*. Now write them again
from an **empty editor**: no starter, no hints, no solution to peek at. The tests are exactly the ones you
Why: in an interview you will be asked to sketch exactly this on a whiteboard, and pulling it out of memory
is what makes it stay there. If you get stuck, go back to the lesson and try again tomorrow.
This check, plus the boss, is what proves the module.

steps.prompt: How many distinct codes do 6 base62 characters give, and is that enough for 6 billion links?
options: About 56.8 billion: enough, but only about 10% sparse, so codes are easy to guess
steps.explain: 62^6 = 56,800,235,584. 6 B links would fill about 10.6% of the space, so a random guess hits a real link about 1 time in 10. Seven characters (3.5 trillion) make guessing far harder.

steps.prompt: Why do most shorteners answer `302` rather than `301`?
options: Browsers can cache a 301 forever, so clicks stop reaching the service and the target can never be changed
A 301 is not allowed to carry a Location header
A 302 is faster for the browser to follow
steps.explain: Control and counting are worth one request per click. A short `Cache-Control: max-age` on the 302 lets the CDN absorb the load without losing that control for long.

steps.title: Cold rebuild: Encode and Decode
prompt: Write `string Encode(long n)` and `long Decode(string code)` for base62 with the alphabet `0-9`, then `a-z`,
- `Decode` reverses it; an empty code or a character outside the alphabet throws `ArgumentException`.
**From memory this time:** the editor starts empty and the tests are the ones you passed in the lesson.
